title: Week 114 · Lesson 138: The Limping Child & Pediatric Musculoskeletal Complaints — FNP-Level Infection, Injury and Growth-Plate Safety
html:
PHASE 5 · FAMILY & LIFESPAN PRIMARY CARE

Week 114 — Lesson 138: The Limping Child & Pediatric Musculoskeletal Complaints

FNP-level goal: Localize pediatric limb and joint symptoms despite referred pain and limited history, distinguish benign overuse from fracture, septic arthritis, osteomyelitis, malignancy, and hip emergencies, select imaging thoughtfully, protect growth plates, and choose safe activity, referral, and emergency disposition.

Learning Objectives

  • Use age, gait, weight-bearing, systemic findings, trauma, and pain timing to build a limp differential.
  • Recognize septic arthritis and osteomyelitis as time-sensitive infections.
  • Identify toddler fracture, slipped capital femoral epiphysis, developmental hip disease, and nonaccidental trauma.
  • Perform an age-appropriate musculoskeletal and neurovascular examination while examining the joints above and below.
  • Use radiography, ultrasound, MRI, laboratory testing, and referral based on the question being asked.

Part 1 — Inability to Bear Weight Is a Signal

Begin with appearance, fever, perfusion, pain severity, deformity, swelling, open injury, neurovascular status, and ability to bear weight. A toxic child, acutely hot swollen joint, severe pain with passive movement, open fracture, absent pulse, compartment signs, or sudden hip pain in a high-risk adolescent requires urgent or emergency evaluation.

Do not assume that a child who cannot describe pain has a minor injury. Observe spontaneous movement and gait before touching the painful area when possible.

Part 2 — Age Organizes the Differential

Infants raise concern for infection, developmental dysplasia, fracture, neurologic disease, or nonaccidental trauma. Toddlers commonly have occult fracture, transient synovitis, infection, or foreign body in the foot. School-age children add overuse, inflammatory disease, Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease, and malignancy. Adolescents add apophyseal injury, stress fracture, slipped capital femoral epiphysis, sports trauma, and pregnancy-related considerations.

The differential remains broad: trauma, infection, inflammation, developmental and orthopedic disease, neurologic disorder, hematologic disease, tumor, and referred abdominal or genitourinary pain.

Part 3 — History That Changes Risk

Ask onset, exact sequence, trauma, recent infection, fever, night pain, morning stiffness, weight loss, fatigue, bruising, rash, tick exposure, travel, sports load, medication, sickle cell disease, immune compromise, prior cancer, and family rheumatologic history. Clarify whether pain precedes the limp and whether symptoms improve during the day.

Night pain that repeatedly wakes a child, constitutional symptoms, unexplained bruising, persistent bone pain, or pain disproportionate to activity raises concern for infection, leukemia, or bone tumor.

Part 4 — Observe and Localize

Watch the child stand, walk, run, turn, and climb if safe. An antalgic gait shortens stance on the painful side. Trendelenburg pattern suggests hip-abductor weakness or hip pathology. Toe walking, circumduction, or foot drop may be neurologic. Refusal to crawl or move one limb may be the infant equivalent of limp.

Examine spine, pelvis, abdomen, and both limbs. Palpate bone and joint lines; assess swelling, warmth, range of motion, strength, sensation, pulses, and skin. Hip disease may present as thigh or knee pain, so always examine the hip when a child reports atraumatic knee pain.

Part 5 — Septic Arthritis

Acute bacterial arthritis often causes fever, severe localized joint pain, limited or absent weight-bearing, effusion, and marked pain with passive motion. Hip involvement may rest in a position of comfort and have little visible swelling. No single clinical score safely replaces judgment.

Obtain blood culture before antibiotics when this does not delay treatment, inflammatory markers for baseline and monitoring, and urgent imaging or aspiration under pediatric orthopedic and infectious-disease pathways. Joint drainage and targeted antibiotics may be required. Delay risks cartilage and growth-plate damage or sepsis.

Part 6 — Osteomyelitis

Acute hematogenous osteomyelitis may produce focal bone pain, tenderness, limp, fever, and reduced use. Early radiographs can be normal but help exclude fracture or tumor. PIDS/IDSA guidance supports blood culture and baseline CRP; MRI is preferred when advanced imaging is needed to define bone, soft-tissue, joint, or abscess involvement.

Pain out of proportion to superficial findings, persistent fever, focal metaphyseal tenderness, or failure of presumed injury to improve should prompt reconsideration. Culture of bone or purulent material can optimize therapy.

Part 7 — Transient Synovitis Is a Diagnosis of Caution

Transient synovitis often follows viral illness and causes hip pain or limp in a well-appearing child with mild restriction. The child is usually afebrile or has low-grade fever and can often bear some weight. Because early septic arthritis can overlap, use appearance, fever, laboratory findings, ultrasound when indicated, and close reassessment.

Worsening pain, fever, inability to bear weight, or failure to improve requires urgent reevaluation rather than repeated reassurance.

Part 8 — Toddler Fracture and Occult Injury

A toddler fracture is often a nondisplaced spiral tibial injury after a minor twist. The child may simply refuse to walk, and initial radiographs may be negative. Localized tibial tenderness and consistent mechanism guide immobilization and follow-up; repeat imaging may reveal healing.

Also assess foot foreign body, stress injury, and nonaccidental trauma. An absent witnessed mechanism does not prove abuse, but injury inconsistent with developmental ability or history requires safeguarding evaluation.

Part 9 — Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis

SCFE usually occurs in adolescents and is associated with increased body mass and endocrine conditions, although any adolescent with compatible symptoms can be affected. Hip, groin, thigh, or knee pain, limp, externally rotated foot, and reduced internal rotation are important clues.

When SCFE is suspected, make the child non-weight-bearing and arrange urgent orthopedic evaluation. Do not force range of motion or allow walking for additional office testing because further slip can worsen avascular necrosis risk.

Part 10 — Perthes and Hip Development

Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease causes avascular necrosis of the femoral head, often presenting in younger school-age children with insidious limp, hip or knee pain, and limited abduction or internal rotation. It requires orthopedic evaluation and longitudinal management.

Developmental dysplasia may be detected by infancy screening or later asymmetry, leg-length difference, limited abduction, or gait change. Early referral improves options; do not rely on a single old normal examination when new signs appear.

Part 11 — Growth Plates and Sports Injury

Children's physes are vulnerable to injury. Focal tenderness over a growth plate after trauma deserves fracture-oriented management even when initial imaging is subtle. Overuse injuries often follow sudden training increases, inadequate rest, technique problems, or low energy availability.

Ask about nutrition, menstrual history when relevant, sleep, pressure to compete, supplements, and safe return to play. Pain that changes gait, persists at rest, or is focal over bone should not be treated with “play through it.”

Part 12 — Compartment and Neurovascular Emergencies

Escalating pain out of proportion, pain with passive stretch, tense swelling, paresthesia, weakness, or deteriorating perfusion suggests compartment syndrome. A normal pulse does not exclude early compartment syndrome. Remove constrictive material and arrange immediate surgical evaluation.

Document pulses, capillary refill, motor and sensory function before and after immobilization.

Part 13 — Safeguarding and Bone Health

Consider nonaccidental trauma with fractures in nonmobile children, multiple healing stages, patterned injury, delay in care, or mechanism incompatible with development. Follow child-protection imaging and reporting protocols; do not confront or conduct repeated interviews.

Recurrent fracture or low-impact fracture may require nutrition, vitamin D, chronic disease, medication, genetic, or endocrine assessment. Avoid assuming that every fracture indicates poor parenting or, conversely, that every unusual fracture is accidental.

Part 14 — Imaging and Follow-Up

Plain radiographs usually begin trauma evaluation and can exclude several diagnoses, but normal films do not rule out early infection, stress fracture, toddler fracture, or cartilage injury. Ultrasound identifies effusion but cannot determine whether fluid is infected. MRI offers sensitive assessment of marrow, soft tissue, abscess, and occult pathology.

Every outpatient plan needs activity limits, immobilization care when used, neurovascular warning signs, analgesia, result ownership, and reassessment timing. Persistent limp without diagnosis should not drift between repeated routine visits.

Clinical Case 1 — Knee Pain From the Hip

A 13-year-old with increased body mass has weeks of knee pain, limp, external rotation, and reduced hip internal rotation. The FNP suspects SCFE, stops weight-bearing, and arranges urgent orthopedic evaluation rather than treating isolated knee strain.

Clinical Case 2 — Fever and Refusal to Walk

A five-year-old has fever, severe hip pain, and refuses weight-bearing; passive motion is extremely painful. The FNP sends the child for emergency septic-arthritis evaluation with cultures, inflammatory markers, imaging, aspiration, and orthopedic coordination.

Clinical Case 3 — Normal First Film

A two-year-old refuses to walk after a minor twisting event and has focal tibial tenderness but normal initial radiographs. The FNP treats suspected occult toddler fracture with appropriate immobilization and follow-up rather than dismissing the pain.

FNP High-Yield Framework: LIMPS

  1. L — Look at the child: stability, gait, weight-bearing, deformity, systemic illness.
  2. I — Identify age and infection risk: fever, immune status, joint versus bone.
  3. M — Map the entire limb: spine, hip, knee, ankle, neurovascular, referred pain.
  4. P — Protect the physis and perfusion: immobilize, non-weight-bearing, compartment awareness.
  5. S — Select imaging and specialist timing: radiograph, ultrasound, MRI, orthopedics, emergency.

Take-Home Summary

A limp is a sign, not a diagnosis. Age and weight-bearing narrow the differential; hip disease can appear as knee pain; early infection and occult fracture may have normal radiographs; and septic arthritis, SCFE, compartment syndrome, neurovascular injury, and suspicious trauma require rapid escalation.

Educational note: Follow current PIDS/IDSA bone-and-joint infection guidance, pediatric orthopedic pathways, imaging criteria, sports protocols, and child-protection law. Toxic appearance, hot immobile joint, severe pain, non-weight-bearing with fever, suspected SCFE, compartment signs, open injury, or neurovascular deficit requires urgent care.
